The second comes from the data.

When the simulation's prior is changed, the data result shifts in correlation with minus the noise-free residual at the same truth (\nsec{sec:gbdt-model-dependence}); these shifts measure the result's sensitivity to the prior (figure~\ref{fig:prior-response}).
The shifts are not a measured bias of the data result.
The correlation supplies no per-cell bias bound (\nsec{sec:gbdt-model-dependence}).

base: This threshold is the larger of 0.05 and 9.03 times the standard deviation of the paired change of $\rho$ over five splits of the simulation.
The factor 9.03 is the two-sided Student-$t$ quantile on four degrees of freedom at a familywise rate of 0.01 over the study's twelve primary comparisons.
The IBU at five iterations is classified according to whether it retains less or more of the prior than the five-observable estimator, using the same rule with its own threshold.
A separate test asks whether its retention falls or rises by at least a fixed margin of 0.05, distinct from that threshold, between five and 200 iterations.
The retained fraction is undefined at a truth where fewer than two cells depart from the prior by at least \SI{1}{\percent}.
A tested level clears a flagged truth if the truth is no longer flagged under the criterion of section~\ref{sec:strategy} applied to the noise-free pseudo-data.

The results are combined into labels fixed in advance: consistent with finite-iteration regularization (more iterations reduce $\rho$, and so do longer IBU runs); consistent with an information limit at these settings (neither more iterations nor more capacity reduces $\rho$, nor do longer IBU runs); and consistent with a share specific to the implementation (the IBU retains less of the prior, or more capacity reduces $\rho$).
The study selects no estimator; its results describe these truths only (\ssec{S9}{supp:tests}).

base: That sensitivity enters the reported statistical block by construction: each of its 50 bootstrap replicas refits the whole unfolding with its own rounding-level perturbation of the inputs.

On the finer joint cells, the rounding spread is about \SI{37}{\percent} of the statistical variance and below a tenth of any total uncertainty (ref.~\cite{AnalysisNote2026}); on the 16 reported cells, over 20 rounding-level perturbations of the data, it is a median \SI{0.133}{\percent} of the cross section (\SIrange{0.055}{0.252}{\percent}); the quoted 2.6 statistical standard deviations is the largest shift, over 153 quantities (the joint cells, the $(\Eavail,W)$ cells and two totals) under two such perturbations of the data, not the typical one.
A probe specified in advance tested two-fold cross-fitting and two tree regularizations on simulated pseudo-data.
No variant met the data-stability requirement, so we retained the estimator (ref.~\cite{AnalysisNote2026}).
Cross-fitting also gives a larger fake-data bias than the current estimator at three of the 17 truths it was graded on.
